summary.text: The continental rise is a low, gently sloping zone of piled-up sediment lying between the continental slope and the abyssal plain.
It builds up as sediment moves downhill under gravity, either gradually or in large sudden slides set off by events such as earthquakes.
Its gradient is usually 1:50 to 1:500, and its sediment layers thin seaward until it merges with the abyssal plain at around 1:1000.

items.prompt: An earthquake shakes loose a mass of sand high on the steep continental slope, and it slides downhill. Where does it mostly come to rest?

options.label: Back up on the shallow shelf
On the crest of a mid-ocean ridge
At the base of the slope, on the rise
Floating in the water near the surface

items.explain: Gravity-driven slides carry sediment down the slope, and it piles up below it, building the continental rise.

items.prompt: Why is the seafloor of the continental rise so much gentler than the continental slope just above it?

options.label: It is built from sediment piled at the slope's foot
It is hard volcanic rock that resists erosion
Ice sheets once scraped it smooth
Strong surface waves keep flattening it

items.explain: The rise lies below the slope and is formed from deposited sediment, which gives it a very gentle slope.

items.prompt: What kind of event commonly sets off a large, sudden slide of sediment onto the rise?

options.label: Warm surface water in summer
A passing ship's wake
Heavy rain falling on the sea
An earthquake shaking the slope

items.explain: Large mass-wasting events are often triggered by sudden events such as earthquakes or an over-steepened continental slope.

items.prompt: The Bengal Fan is one of the largest sediment structures in the world. Roughly how far does it stretch?

options.label: About 30 kilometres
About 3,000 kilometres
About 300 metres
About 30,000 kilometres

items.explain: The Bengal Fan stretches about 3,000 kilometres (1,900 miles), making it one of the world's largest sedimentary structures.

items.prompt: Energy companies and scientists gather seismic data over the sediment fans at the base of the continental slope. What makes these fans worth the effort?

options.label: They are where most earthquakes begin
They hide large stores of fresh water
Many hold oil and natural gas reservoirs
They are the main feeding grounds of whales

items.explain: Many of these fans contain critical oil and natural gas reservoirs, so they are key places for collecting seismic data.

items.prompt: Travelling seaward across the continental rise, away from the slope, what happens to the layers of sediment beneath you?

options.label: They grow thicker and steeper
They stay exactly the same
They turn into fresh volcanic rock
They thin out as the rise meets the plain

items.explain: As the rise extends seaward its sediment layers thin, and it merges with the abyssal plain.

paragraphs.heading: A ramp of sediment
paragraphs.text: The continental rise is a zone of gentle relief, made of piled-up sediment, lying between the continental slope and the abyssal plain. It is a major part of the continental margin and covers around 10% of the ocean floor. Its sediments are mostly silt and clay. Because it sits below the slope and is built by sediment settling out, it slopes very gently, usually between 1:50 and 1:500.

paragraphs.heading: How the sediment arrives
paragraphs.text: The rise grows as sediment is laid down, mostly through mass wasting, which is the downhill movement of sand and other sediment under gravity. Mass wasting can be slow, with sediment building up in fits and starts, or it can come in large, sudden events. The big ones are often set off by earthquakes or by the slope above becoming too steep. Slower build-up happens when hemipelagic sediment hanging in the seawater gradually sinks to the ocean basin.

paragraphs.heading: Fans at the foot of the slope
paragraphs.text: Where submarine canyons open out, sediment can heap up into enormous fan-shaped piles called submarine fans, on both the slope and the rise. These fans are shallow cone-shaped mounds at the base of the slope, and as neighbouring fans merge they form the continental rise. Canyons carved by erosion run downhill into fan valleys that get deeper as they go, and it is in this zone that the sediment of the rise is dropped.

paragraphs.heading: A giant example
paragraphs.text: The Bengal Fan stretches 3,000 kilometers and ranks among the largest sedimentary structures in the world. Many fans like it hold important oil and natural gas reservoirs. That makes them key spots for gathering seismic data.

paragraphs.heading: Out to the abyssal plain
paragraphs.text: Moving seaward, the sediment layers of the rise thin out and it blends into the abyssal plain, usually at a gradient of about 1:1000. The abyssal plain rests on basaltic oceanic crust and spans most of the seafloor. Its creatures are uniquely suited to the cold, the high pressure and the dark. Its flatness is broken by huge underwater mountain chains near the boundaries of Earth's tectonic plates.
